brief_summary:
Why is this study conducted? The purpose of this study is to improve treatment efficacy, particularly the pathological complete response rate, in patients with high-risk/extremely high-risk locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC). While advances have been achieved with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy combined with immunotherapy in recent years, regional recurrence and distant metastasis remain unresolved. New therapeutic strategies for this patient population are therefore urgently needed.

Rectal cancer management typically includes surgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy. Treatment paradigms are shifting toward neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy plus immunotherapy, which has demonstrated promising potential in several clinical trials. These data indicate that short-course radiotherapy combined with anti-angiogenic agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors may improve patient prognosis and tumor response. Nevertheless, the efficacy and safety of this regimen in high-risk patients require further validation.

Against this background, the study evaluates a novel regimen of short-course radiotherapy followed by surufatinib and toripalimab (anti-PD-1) to raise the pathological complete response rate. The investigators also explore efficacy-related biomarkers including RAS/BRAF status and gene expression profiles to support personalized treatment. This study aims to optimize therapy for LARC patients and inform future treatment strategies.

Why are participants invited to participate in this study? Participants are considered eligible for enrollment upon diagnosis of high-risk or extremely high-risk locally advanced rectal cancer consistent with study inclusion criteria. Eligibility requires confirmed pathological diagnosis, appropriate tumor location, and absence of severe comorbidities or exclusionary diseases (e.g., recurrent rectal cancer, cardiac dysfunction). Final enrollment decisions are made by study physicians based on individual clinical conditions.

What do participants need to do to participate in this study? Study participation requires adherence to predefined procedures. Participants receive scheduled medical assessments including blood tests, imaging scans and anorectal function evaluation. During the study period, participants may complete questionnaires and provide biospecimens (e.g., blood samples) for efficacy analysis. The study team defines the frequency and content of each follow-up to maintain continuous monitoring throughout treatment. Compliance with study procedures supports evaluation of regimen efficacy.

What are the risks of participating in this study?

This study applies neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy, anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody (toripalimab), and anti-angiogenic therapy (surufatinib). Potential risks for participants are listed below:

Risk of neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy: Participants may develop grade ≥3 adverse events including, but not limited to, severe diarrhea, grade 3 neutropenia and grade 3 radiation dermatitis, which may impair quality of life.

Risk of anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody: Toripalimab may induce immune-related adverse events (irAEs) across organ systems. Common irAEs include skin toxicity (papules, pruritus; incidence 30%-40%), diarrhea/colitis (8%-19%), fatigue (16%-24%), immune-related hepatitis (5%), hypothyroidism (4%-10%), and hyperthyroidism (4%). Approximately two-thirds of patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors develop irAEs of varying severity, and serious adverse events are non-negligible.

Risk of anti-angiogenic therapy: Surufatinib may trigger adverse events related to anti-angiogenic and immunomodulatory effects. Common adverse events (incidence \>20%) include proteinuria, hypertension, bleeding, liver dysfunction and diarrhea. Among grade ≥3 adverse events, hypertension (29.7%), proteinuria (14.5%), liver dysfunction (12.8%) and bleeding (4.5%) predominate. Rarely, treatment-related death may occur secondary to gastrointestinal hemorrhage or cerebral hemorrhage.

Handling of research related injuries? This interventional study introduces no extra risks beyond standard clinical care. Any harm arising from study participation will be addressed for compensation and liability in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.
lead_sponsor: The First Hospital of Jilin University
title: Efficacy and Safety Exploration of Short Course Radiotherapy Followed by Surufatinib and Toripalimab in Neoadjuvant Treatment of Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer

brief_summary:
Caring for a family member after a hip fracture can place physical, emotional, social, and financial demands on the main caregiver. This study evaluates whether a support program based on the Family-Centered Empowerment Model can reduce caregiver burden compared with usual care. The program helps caregivers understand care needs, develop practical skills, build confidence, and involve other family members in caregiving.

The study plans to include 80 adult family caregivers of patients with hip fracture at one hospital in China, with 40 caregivers in each group. Group assignment depends on the enrollment period rather than chance. Caregivers enrolled during the earlier period receive usual orthopedic care guidance and follow-up. Those enrolled during the later period receive the same usual care plus the empowerment program, including education, practical skills training, family discussions, and support after discharge.

Caregivers complete questionnaires near the patient's hospital admission, at discharge, and at 1 and 3 months after discharge. The main outcome is caregiver burden, meaning the strain and difficulties associated with providing care. Other outcomes include confidence in managing challenges, self-esteem, and caregiving-related quality of life. Patient complications and hospital readmissions are also recorded. The study will assess whether adding the empowerment program improves these outcomes.
interventions: Usual Orthopedic Care Guidance and Follow-up
lead_sponsor: The Fourth Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine
primary_outcomes: Caregiver Burden Measured by the Zarit Burden Interview (ZBI)
title: Application of the Family-Centered Empowerment Model in an Intervention to Reduce Burden Among Primary Caregivers of Patients With Hip Fracture

brief_summary:
Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy characterized by substantial variability in clinical severity, functional recovery, and pain outcomes. The lack of validated and accessible prognostic biomarkers limits early risk stratification and individualized rehabilitation strategies.

This observational, longitudinal, retrospective and prospective study aims to evaluate a panel of five blood biomarkers (EGR1, EGR2, GBP1, miR-29c, and Piccolo) and determine their association with functional recovery, pain trajectories, and neurophysiological characteristics in patients with GBS.

The study will include at least 70 patients with GBS and 70 healthy controls. Patients will undergo longitudinal clinical and molecular assessments across different disease stages, whereas healthy controls will provide a single blood sample for reference measurements. Gene and microRNA expression will be quantified using quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), and serum Piccolo concentrations will be assessed using ELISA or validated immunoassays.

Clinical assessments will include the GBS Disability Scale, Medical Research Council (MRC) Sum Score, Functional Independence Measure (FIM), and validated pain questionnaires. Molecular and clinical data will be integrated using multivariable statistical analyses to identify prognostic molecular signatures and develop predictive models.

The project also aims to support external validation in Mexican populations through international collaboration with Spanish research institutions.
interventions: Blood Biomarker Panel Assessment (EGR1, EGR2, GBP1, miR-29c, and Piccolo)
primary_outcomes: Change in Guillain-Barré Syndrome Disability Score
Change in Muscle Strength Assessed by the MRC Sum Score
title: Blood Biomarkers for Prognostic Stratification in Guillain-Barré Syndrome

brief_summary: Flexor tendon injuries of hand requires precise and strong repair to achieve healing without rupture and gap formation with sufficient strength and excursion for daily activities. The choice of flexor tendon repair technique depends on various factors including surgeon preference, required tensile strength and zone of the hand involved. Various types of four strand techniques are widely used because they provide greater tensile strength and better stability. Core suture configuration has key importance in ultimate outcome of tendon repair. Modification of McLarney cruciate technique into cross locking suture pattern (Adelaide technique) is believed to offer better results. This study is being conducted to compare the clinical outcomes between these two techniques including total arc of motion (TAM), grip strength and rate of complications. It is hypothesized that four-strand cross locked cruciate technique ensures better clinical outcomes. This study will be conducted in department of Plastic Surgery, Nishtar Hospital, Multan. A total of 30 patients will be inducted fulfilling the inclusion criteria and will be randomized into two groups preoperatively. Group A n=30 will be operated by using cruciate cross locked (Adelaide) technique while Group B n=30 will be operated by using four strand McLarney cruciate technique. All patients will follow the early active place and hold rehabilitation protocol post operatively. Patients will be assessed at 2,4,8 weeks for any complication and at 12 weeks and at 6 months for total arc of motion (TAM) while grip strength will be assessed at 6th month. The patients will be followed weekly for compliance of proposed rehabilitation protocol to ensure strict compliance. The result of this study helps in making informed decision regarding appropriate repair technique for flexor tendon injuries.
conditions: Flexor Tendon Repair of Zone 2 of Hand
interventions: Four-strand cross-locked cruciate (Adelaide) flexor tendon repair
Four-strand McLarney cruciate flexor tendon repair
primary_outcomes: Total Active Motion (TAM) of the distal and proximal interphalangeal (DIP and PIP) joints
title: Adelaide vs McLarney Four-strand Repair for Zone 2 Flexor Tendon Injuries

brief_summary: The goal of this non-randomized clinical study is to learn whether an intragastric balloon (IGB) and time-restricted eating (TRE; 16-hour daily fast with an 8-hour eating window), used alone or together, improve weight loss, body composition, and metabolic parameters in adults aged 18 to 65 years with overweight or obesity (body mass index 27.0 to 39.9 kg/m²). All participants receive the same individualized energy-restricted diet, dietitian follow-up, behavioral education, and physical activity advice. Body weight and body composition are measured at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months; routine laboratory results are recorded at baseline and 6 months.
title: Intragastric Balloon and Time-Restricted Eating for Weight Loss in Adults With Overweight or Obesity

brief_summary:
The goal of this pilot clinical trial is to learn whether continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) with real-time glucose feedback and personalized nutrition education can improve dietary choices, caloric intake, and cardiometabolic health in adults ages 55-75 years who are overweight or obese and do not have diabetes. The study will also examine participants' experiences using CGM, including its usability and effects on motivation and dietary behaviors.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does access to real-time CGM feedback combined with personalized nutrition education improve dietary choices and eating behaviors compared with blinded CGM use without access to glucose data or nutrition education?
* Does real-time CGM feedback combined with personalized nutrition education improve cardiometabolic health, including glucose regulation, insulin sensitivity, blood lipids, and other metabolic biomarkers?
* Does real-time CGM feedback combined with personalized nutrition education influence behavioral and physiological indicators of metabolic health, including meal frequency, eating window, physical activity, metabolic hormones, and inflammatory biomarkers?

Researchers will compare participants' dietary intake and glucose patterns during two weeks of blinded CGM use, when participants cannot see their glucose data and receive no nutrition guidance, with four weeks of unblinded CGM use, when participants can view their glucose data and receive personalized nutrition education.

Participants will:

* Wear a CMG for six weeks, first without access to their glucose readings and then with real-time access to their glucose data.
* Receive personalized nutrition education during the unblinded CGM phase focused on reducing post-meal glucose spikes through changes in meal composition, portion size, and meal timing. CGM proposal
* Complete dietary recalls to measure changes in food choices and caloric intake.
* Complete baseline and post-intervention assessments, including blood tests, body composition, resting metabolic rate, physical function, and questionnaires.
* Complete questionnaires about CGM usability, barriers and facilitators to CGM use, motivation, and health-related quality of life.
title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Dietary Choices and Cardiometabolic Health in Older Adults Without Diabetes

brief_summary:
This study will explore how, why and under what circumstances acute children's hospital settings support, or fail to support Black and Mixed-Black children and young people (CYP) to access appropriate mental health (MH) support. This matters because more CYP with MH issues are attending acute children's hospital settings. These settings include emergency departments and children's wards. Investigations have shown that they are often unsuitable for managing high-risk MH behaviour. CYP from ethnic minority groups have poorer access to, and outcomes from, MH services, but they remain under-researched. Black ethnic groups, in particular, have had persistently higher rates of serious mental health issues and detention under the Mental Health Act.

This study will use an exploratory mixed-methods multiple case study design. It will take place across up to three acute hospital trusts in England, including Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust and University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust. Data collection methods will include document reviews, observations, interviews, patient record reviews and anonymised aggregate statistics about CYP's MH presentations.

The study will use purposive sampling and aims to recruit about 90 participants: around 30 CYP, 30 parents or carers, and 30 healthcare professionals. Recruitment may take place through posters containing QR codes displayed in hospitals, community and mental health organisations, and on social media. Children, young people, and parents/carers may also be identified by clinical staff during an acute hospital presentation or through hospital databases following discharge. Healthcare professionals may additionally be recruited through email invitations, staff meetings, and direct approaches.

People who express interest, or complete a consent-to-contact form, will be contacted by the researcher to confirm whether they are eligible and to arrange an information session. Consent will usually be completed electronically. The University of Leicester is sponsoring this research as part of a PhD fellowship funded by the Wellcome Trust.
primary_outcomes: Qualitative experiences and perceptions of how acute paediatric settings support or do not support access to mental health support - interviews.

brief_summary:
The primary aim of this study is to determine the serum amyloid A (SAA) family protein levels in gingival tissue samples obtained from periodontally healthy and periodontitis patients and to evaluate their relationship with periodontal status. Additionally, the study aims to assess the potential effect of smoking on the amount of SAA proteins in gingival tissue.

Following ethical committee approval, a total of 108 individuals aged 18-65 years who attending to the Department of Periodontology, Biruni University Faculty of Dentistry, will be included in the study. The study groups will consist of 27 non-smoking individuals with periodontally healthy tissue, 27 smoking individuals with periodontally healthy tissue, 27 non-smoking individuals with stage III grade B periodontitis, and 27 smoking individuals with stage III grade C periodontitis. The non-smoking groups will include individuals who have never smoked, while the smoking groups will include individuals who, according to patient statements, have smoked at least 10 cigarettes per day for more than five years.

All participants will be informed about the study and their written consent will be obtained. Plaque score, probing depth, gingival margin position, clinical attachment level, and bleeding on probing will be measured by a calibrated investigator. Gingival tissue samples from periodontally healthy individuals will be collected during planned tooth extraction or periodontal surgical procedures such as gingivoplasty, gingivectomy, or clinical crown lengthening, independent of the study. Only gingival tissues that would otherwise be discarded as medical waste during routine treatment will be used. In individuals with periodontitis, granulation tissue removed during subgingival instrumentation as part of non-surgical periodontal treatment is planned for use. No additional tissue will be removed from the periodontal pocket wall or junctional epithelium for research purposes; the scope of the clinical procedure will not be expanded if suitable tissue cannot be obtained.

Gingival tissue samples will only be collected initially, stored at -80°C until the day of analysis, and evaluated using the ELISA method.
title: Evaluation of Gingival Tissue Protein Levels of Serum Amyloid A Family Members

brief_summary:

This single-centre cross-sectional study, conducted among adults living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy at the HIV clinic of Hospital Universitario San Ignacio in Bogotá, Colombia, aimed to estimate the prevalence of HPV infection and cytological abnormalities in the anus, cervix and oropharynx; to describe high-risk HPV genotype distribution at each site; and, within the anal component, to explore factors associated with high-risk HPV detection and the agreement between anal cytology and HPV genotyping. Participants were selected by simple random sampling from eligible adults attending the HIV clinic, and liquid-based cytology and extended high-risk HPV genotyping were performed on anal, cervical (when applicable), and oropharyngeal samples.
primary_outcomes: Prevalence of High-Risk HPV Infection by Anatomical Site
Distribution of high-risk HPV genotypes by anatomical site
Prevalence of cytological abnormalities by anatomical site

brief_summary:
Rib fractures are a common cause of acute pain after blunt chest trauma. In the emergency department, pain is usually managed with a multimodal approach including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), opioids, local anesthetic sprays, patches and nerve blocks. Systemic analgesics may cause gastrointestinal, renal and hepatic adverse effects, and opioids carry the risk of respiratory depression and dependence. External chest wall stabilization with a rib orthosis may reduce pain by stabilizing the fracture with fewer systemic adverse effects.

This randomized, open-label, controlled trial compares the Chrisofix Chest Orthosis (CCO) combined with ibuprofen versus ibuprofen alone in adult patients presenting to the emergency department with fewer than three rib fractures. Pain intensity (Numeric Rating Scale), functional limitation, analgesic consumption and adverse events are assessed during emergency department observation and during a 7-day post-discharge follow-up.

PreCharge is a personalized online support program for people with a hereditary cancer syndrome. The study is for adults who have not had cancer, with an exception for non-melanoma skin cancer.

The main question the study aims to answer is:

• Does PreCharge help participants feel more confident in their ability to cope with their inherited cancer risk? Researchers will compare participants who use PreCharge with participants who do not use the program during the study. Researchers will also look at participants' resilience, anxiety, depressive symptoms, cancer worry, and overall well-being.

Participants will be assigned by chance to one of two groups. Participants in both groups will answer online surveys at the start of the study and about 3 and 6 months later.

Progressive muscle relaxation is a non-pharmacological technique that involves systematically tensing and relaxing different muscle groups to promote physical relaxation and reduce discomfort.

The study includes 96 elderly patients with diabetes mellitus who are divided into two groups. The intervention group receives progressive muscle relaxation in addition to routine care, while the control group receives routine care alone.

brief_summary:
The goal of this randomized controlled clinical trial is to compare the effectiveness of topical Permethrin 5% cream and Spinosad 0.9% suspension in treating scabies in patients aged 5-60 years.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Is there a difference in the effectiveness of topical Permethrin 5% and Spinosad 0.9% in treating scabies at Day 14?
* What are the treatment-related adverse effects of these two medications?

Researchers will compare the two treatment groups to determine whether there is a significant difference in treatment efficacy.

Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups:

* Group A will receive topical Permethrin 5% cream, applied from the neck to the toes for 8-12 hours, followed by washing. A second application will be given after 7 days.
* Group B will receive topical Spinosad 0.9% suspension, applied similarly, with repeat application only if clinically indicated.

Participants will be instructed regarding correct treatment application, hygiene measures, and treatment of close contacts. They will be assessed at baseline, Day 7, and Day 14.

The main outcome will be treatment efficacy at Day 14, defined as complete resolution of itching, healing of skin lesions, and absence of new lesions.
primary_outcomes: Proportion of participants achieving treatment efficacy at day 14

brief_summary:
Following tooth extraction, a series of sequential events occurs, leading to significant qualitative and quantitative changes at the edentulous site. The socket healing process results in dimensional alterations of both the underlying bone and the overlying soft tissue architecture. The loss of soft tissue contour following tooth extraction may persist even after the healing process, irrespective of the application of alveolar ridge preservation techniques. Consequently, clinicians are exploring various surgical methods to address the loss of hard and soft tissue volume post-extraction.

Immediately following tooth extraction, biological processes are initiated that lead to bone resorption and subsequent changes in soft tissue contour. A recent systematic review on post-extraction alveolar hard and soft tissue alterations in humans reported horizontal changes ranging from 29% to 63% after 6 to 7 months . The percentage of vertical changes was less pronounced, ranging from 11% to 22%
interventions: Ridge preservation using socket seal with modified free gingival graft and xenograft.

brief_summary:
This study tests the safety and feasibility of a new type of brain-computer interface (BCI) in people with severe paralysis caused by stroke, spinal cord injury, or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). A BCI records signals directly from the brain and uses them to control external devices. In this study, a small stent-shaped sensor (a metal mesh tube carrying tiny electrodes) is placed inside a vein on the surface of the brain through a needle puncture in a large vein below the collarbone, so no open-brain surgery is needed. Once in place, the sensor records brain activity while participants imagine or attempt movements.

Two participants will be enrolled. One participant with stroke-related arm paralysis who still has rehabilitation potential will receive closed-loop functional electrical stimulation (FES): when the BCI detects the intention to move the paralyzed hand, electrical pulses are delivered to the arm muscles, producing real movement and sensory feedback. This pairing of intention and movement may help the brain rebuild damaged pathways. The other participant with ALS or severe paraplegia and no realistic chance of recovering voluntary movement will use the same sensor to control a robotic arm that helps perform daily tasks such as eating, grasping objects, and opening a door.

For both participants, the study lasts about 60 days after sensor implantation. Training sessions last 45 minutes per day during weeks 2 to 4. Imaging (brain CT and CT venography), electroencephalography (EEG), blood tests, and movement or daily-living assessments are performed at regular intervals. After the week-4 evaluation, the sensor is either removed (short-term group) or left in place for continued monitoring (long-term group), based on the participant's own choice made before enrollment and on clinical judgment. The main measures are safety (side effects, blood clots, bleeding, device problems), quality of the recorded brain signals, accuracy of decoding movement intention, and improvement in arm function or daily-task performance.
conditions: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis & Other Neuromuscular Disorders
primary_outcomes: Effective Signal Bandwidth of the Endovascular Sensor
title: Endovascular Brain-Computer Interface for Upper-Limb Paralysis

brief_summary:
This study aims to investigate the therapeutic efficacy and neural mechanisms of individualized neuromodulation combined with autobiographical Think/No-Think (TNT) thought suppression training in individuals with internalizing disorders, including anxiety disorders, depressive disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), including complex PTSD (cPTSD).

Internalizing disorders share common clinical features, including excessive negative emotional processing, impaired regulation of intrusive thoughts and memories, and difficulties in cognitive control. Increasing evidence suggests that impaired thought suppression is a transdiagnostic mechanism contributing to persistent negative thoughts, intrusive memories, rumination, and emotional dysregulation across different psychiatric conditions. However, effective interventions targeting this shared cognitive mechanism remain limited.

This study is designed to examine whether individualized neuromodulation targeting abnormal neural circuits and oscillatory activity can enhance thought suppression ability and improve clinical symptoms. The study is based on the hypothesis that dysfunction of prefrontal-limbic and memory-related networks, including altered interactions between prefrontal cortex, hippocampal, and amygdala-related circuits, contributes to impaired cognitive control over unwanted thoughts and memories. Furthermore, individual differences in neural oscillatory characteristics may provide biomarkers for optimizing neuromodulation parameters.

Eligible participants with internalizing disorders will undergo comprehensive clinical assessments, behavioral assessments, electroencephalography (EEG), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) evaluations before intervention. Behavioral assessment will include an autobiographical Think/No-Think (TNT) paradigm designed to measure participants' ability to intentionally regulate retrieval of unwanted autobiographical memories. EEG and MRI assessments will be used to characterize individual neural oscillatory features and functional brain network characteristics associated with cognitive control, emotional regulation, and memory processing.

Participants will be randomly assigned to one of five parallel intervention groups according to the study protocol:

Individualized temporal interference stimulation (TIS) combined with autobiographical TNT thought suppression training; Individualized beta-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) combined with autobiographical TNT thought suppression training; Sham neuromodulation combined with autobiographical TNT thought suppression training; Individualized beta-frequency tACS alone; Individualized TIS alone.

The first neuromodulation approach, individualized tACS, targets the right anterior dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (aDLPFC), a key region involved in cognitive control and thought suppression. The stimulation frequency will be individualized according to each participant's resting-state EEG beta-band peak characteristics.

The second neuromodulation approach, individualized TIS, aims to modulate deep brain networks involved in emotional memory regulation and cognitive control. TIS stimulation parameters will be individualized according to participant-specific neurophysiological characteristics, with a focus on theta-related neural activity associated with limbic and memory-related circuits.

During the combined intervention conditions, individualized tACS or TIS will be administered concurrently with autobiographical TNT training. Participants will practice intentionally retrieving autobiographical memories during Think trials and suppressing retrieval of unwanted autobiographical memories during No-Think trials. The tACS-only and TIS-only groups will receive the corresponding individualized neuromodulation intervention without TNT training, allowing evaluation of the independent effects of neuromodulation and comparison with combined neuromodulation-cognitive training approaches. Sham stimulation combined with TNT training will serve as a control condition for evaluating the specific contribution of active neuromodulation.

The intervention period will last six days according to the study protocol. Clinical symptoms, thought suppression ability, emotional regulation, and behavioral performance will be assessed before and after intervention. Additional clinical follow-up assessments will be conducted at one month and six months after intervention to evaluate the durability of treatment effects.EEG and MRI assessments will be performed before and after intervention to investigate neurophysiological and neural network changes associated with treatment response.
primary_outcomes: Change in Emotional Responses to Personally Relevant Events
title: Efficacy and Neural Mechanisms of Individualized Neuromodulation Combined With Think/No-Think Training in Individuals With Internalizing Disorders

brief_summary:
KRP-203 is an experimental medicine taken as a capsule. It keeps some white blood cells (lymphocytes) inside the lymph nodes, so fewer circulate in the blood. It may help treat diseases where the immune system attacks the body, such as ulcerative colitis. After earlier studies in the United Kingdom, this study tested KRP-203 for the first time in healthy Japanese adults.

What did the study want to find out?

The main goal was to learn how safe and well tolerated KRP-203 is after one dose and after daily doses for 28 days. It also measured how much medicine gets into the blood, how long it stays, and its effect on lymphocyte counts and heart rate.

Who could take part?

Healthy Japanese men and women aged 20 to 55 years with a body mass index of 18.5 to under 25. Women could only take part if they could not become pregnant. People could not take part if they smoked, took regular medicines, or had heart rhythm problems, lung disease, eye swelling (macular edema), allergies, immune disease, liver or kidney disease, or infections such as hepatitis or HIV.

How was the study done?

The study had 2 parts at one center in Japan. In each group, participants were assigned by chance to KRP-203 or placebo (a dummy capsule). Neither participants nor study doctors knew who received which.

Part 1 (single dose): 40 people in 4 groups of 10 (8 KRP-203, 2 placebo) received one dose of 0.3, 1, 2 or 3 mg. Each higher dose followed a safety review. Participants stayed at the center for 7 days, with check-ups up to Day 15.

Part 2 (daily doses): 24 people in 2 groups of 12 (9 KRP-203, 3 placebo) took 1.2 or 2 mg once a day for 28 days, after Part 1 was completed safely. Participants stayed at the center for 32 days, with check-ups up to Day 49.

Everyone received a placebo capsule the day before the first dose for baseline measurements.

What tests were done?

Health checks, blood pressure, heart rate, ECG and 24-hour heart monitoring, blood and urine tests, breathing tests and nerve checks. Part 2 participants also had eye examinations.

What were the possible risks? In earlier studies, KRP-203 slowed the heart rate, mainly in the first hours after the first dose, and sometimes caused a temporary heart rhythm disturbance at higher doses. Other effects included headache, tiredness, nausea, and temporary changes in breathing and liver tests. Fewer lymphocytes may increase the risk of infection. Men had to use reliable contraception until 3 months after the study.

brief_summary:
Overview:

Depression is common among Veterans. About 1 in 6 Veterans experiences depression at any given time, and about half may experience it during their lifetime. Without treatment, depression can contribute to substance use, poor health, suicide, and early death. However, many people delay or do not receive treatment. Fewer than one-third of Veterans with depression use psychotherapy. Although the VA is working to improve access to mental health care, staffing shortages can lead to long wait times. These waiting periods may provide an opportunity to support Veterans and help them prepare for treatment.

Mental Health Link:

The research team developed Mental Health Link (MHL), a text-based process that supports Veterans while they wait for mental health services. MHL helps patients better understand their emotions and symptoms and offers simple coping strategies they can use right away while waiting.

Study Goals:

The study will examine whether MHL helps Veterans during the wait period and with treatment engagement. The study will also ask Veterans and providers about what helps or prevents MHL from being used in routine care.

Study Design:

Over five years, the study will compare MHL with usual care at three VA sites. It will include 192 Veterans referred to psychotherapy for depression. The results will show whether MHL improves participation in treatment and helps Veterans while they wait for services.

In the future, these findings may help the VA expand MHL and other effective mental health and suicide-prevention services.
lead_sponsor: VA Office of Research and Development
primary_outcomes: Effectiveness of Intervention as Assessed by Rate of Depression Treatment Initiation
Effectiveness of Intervention as Assessed by Rate of Depression Treatment Adherence
Barriers and Facilitators of Mental Health Link (MHL) Future Implementation

Recruitment began in 2024, enrolling families from late pregnancy through the child's first 6 years of life, with a target of at least 1000- 1200 children and their families.

The study characterizes longitudinal microbiome trajectories-including resilience and dysbiosis-and their relationship to common chronic diseases. Data are collected via online surveys, symptom and medication diaries, annual clinical exams, and repeated biological sampling of the child, mother, father/partner, siblings, and household environment. Findings are intended to support future diagnostics, prevention, and therapy for common chronic physical and mental diseases.

brief_summary:
ProMuscle2025 is a prospective, randomized, open-label, two-parallel-group, post-marketing clinical trial designed to evaluate the efficacy, tolerability, and safety of an HMB-enriched protein module in adults with insufficient protein intake and/or increased protein requirements. Disease-related malnutrition and sarcopenia are characterized by progressive loss of muscle mass and strength, impaired physical function, and poorer clinical outcomes. Inadequate protein intake is a major contributor to this process. Beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate (HMB), an active metabolite of leucine, has anabolic and anti-catabolic properties and may support muscle protein synthesis and preservation of lean tissue. However, additional controlled clinical evidence is needed in nutritionally vulnerable patients with heterogeneous chronic conditions.

The study will be conducted in adults aged ≥18 years attending the Endocrinology and Nutrition Department of Hospital Universitario Virgen de la Victoria, Málaga, Spain. Eligible participants must have increased protein requirements and/or nutritional risk with protein needs not adequately covered, be able to perform the planned functional tests, and provide written informed consent. Participants with severe or decompensated comorbidities, allergy to study-product components, current participation in another clinical trial, or ongoing supplementation with HMB-containing products will be excluded.

Participants will be randomly assigned using a computerized system to either an experimental group or a comparator group. Both groups will receive a nutritional and physical-exercise program according to routine clinical practice. In addition, the experimental group will receive the HMB-enriched protein module ProSup Protein® at a dose individualized according to the participant's protein requirements. The comparator group will receive standard nutritional management, ensuring that nutritional requirements are adequately covered. The recruitment period is planned for 6 months, and each participant will be followed for 3 months, with assessments at baseline, a telephone visit at 1.5 months, and a final in-person visit at 3 months.

The main outcomes will assess changes in physical function, muscle composition, and nutritional status. Functional assessment will include handgrip and quadriceps dynamometry, the Timed Up and Go test, sit-to-stand tests, and 20-repetition-maximum performance. Muscle and body-composition assessment will include rectus femoris ultrasound and bioelectrical impedance vector analysis, including body cell mass, phase angle, standardized phase angle, fat-free mass index, appendicular skeletal muscle index, and skeletal muscle index. Disease-related malnutrition and sarcopenia will be evaluated using GLIM and EWGSOP2 criteria, respectively. Secondary outcomes will include adherence to supplementation and product tolerability, including adverse events.

The target recruitment is 118 participants, allowing for an estimated 20% attrition and aiming for 98 evaluable participants (49 per group). Analyses will include intention-to-treat and per-protocol approaches, repeated-measures comparisons, and multivariable models. The study aims to determine whether an HMB-enriched protein module can improve muscle function, body composition, and nutritional status while maintaining good adherence, tolerability, and safety compared with standard nutritional care.
lead_sponsor: Fundación Pública Andaluza para la Investigación de Málaga en Biomedicina y Salud
title: Protein Supplement in Patients With Insufficient Protein Intake and/or Increased Requirements.

brief_summary:
Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GT) is a serious inherited bleeding disorder. In GT, platelets, the blood cells that normally stick together at the site of an injury to stop bleeding, are unable to properly do so. As a result, bleeding does not stop as it should. Bleeding in GT often starts without warning, can happen frequently, and can be severe. It most commonly affects the nose, mouth and gums, gastrointestinal tract, and skin, and many women and girls with GT experience heavy menstrual bleeding. Over time, bleeding can lead to iron deficiency and anemia. Some bleeding episodes require emergency care, hospitalization, transfusion, or surgery, and some can be life-threatening.

Sutacimig is an investigational medicine given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection). It is designed to help platelets work at the site of bleeding despite the underlying defect in GT. It is intended to be given regularly to help prevent bleeding (prophylaxis), rather than only to treat bleeding after it starts.

The purpose of this study is to find out whether sutacimig, given as prophylaxis, reduces the number of treated bleeding episodes in people with GT compared with no prophylaxis, and to evaluate its safety and tolerability.
title: A Phase 3 Evaluation of Sutacimig in Glanzmann Thrombasthenia

brief_summary:
This study aims to evaluate changes in halitosis and olfactory function in adults with advanced dental caries requiring tooth extraction.

A total of 80 adult patients aged 18-65 years with one or more teeth indicated for extraction due to advanced dental caries will be included. Tooth extractions will be performed under local anesthesia using an atraumatic technique as part of routine dental care. The extraction sockets will be allowed to heal by secondary intention.

Assessments will be performed before tooth extraction and 21 days after the last extraction. Halitosis will be evaluated by a single trained and blinded examiner using the organoleptic scoring method (OLS). Participants will also rate their perceived halitosis using a visual analog scale (VAS).

Olfactory function will be assessed using the Sniffin' Sticks test, which consists of three components: odor threshold, odor discrimination, and odor identification. The scores of these three tests will be combined to calculate the total TDI score.

The preoperative and postoperative results will be compared to investigate changes in halitosis and olfactory function following the removal of carious teeth.
primary_outcomes: Change in Organoleptic Score (OLS) from Baseline to Follow-up

brief_summary:
This is a double-blind, sham-controlled randomized study to test whether theta transcranial alternating current stimulation (theta tACS) at 4.5 Hz or 6 Hz, added to standard clinical care, improves symptoms of schizophrenia and is safe and well tolerated. Approximately 150 adults aged 18 to 60 years with schizophrenia will be randomly assigned equally to one of three groups: active 4.5 Hz tACS, active 6 Hz tACS, or sham tACS. Both participants and outcome assessors will be masked to group assignment.

All participants will continue their usual clinical treatment. They will receive one 40-minute tACS session per day over 10 working days (10 sessions total). Symptom assessments will take place at baseline, immediately after the stimulation period, Day 30, and Day 56. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans will be collected at baseline and post-stimulation. Adverse events will be monitored throughout the study.

The primary goal is to compare whether active theta tACS leads to a greater reduction in overall schizophrenia symptoms from baseline to Day 15 relative to sham tACS. Secondary assessments include symptom changes at other follow-up time points, changes in specific symptom domains, treatment completion rate, safety, and brain imaging changes.
primary_outcomes: Change From Baseline in Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) Total Score at Day 15
title: θTACS for Schizophrenia (SCZ)

brief_summary: This is a randomized controlled trial to investigate whether a combination of Polygonatum odoratum extract and aerobic exercise can improve body composition, insulin resistance, and inflammation in men with central obesity. Participants will be randomly assigned to either an intervention group (90 days of supervised aerobic exercise combined with daily Polygonatum odoratum extract supplementation) or a control group (usual lifestyle advice). The investigators will measure changes in body fat percentage, muscle mass, blood glucose, insulin levels, inflammatory markers, gut microbiota, and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) before and after the 90-day intervention. The goal is to evaluate whether combining Polygonatum odoratum supplementation with aerobic exercise can improve metabolic health in men with central obesity. Possible benefits include improved body composition and insulin sensitivity, as well as favorable changes in gut microbiota and SCFA profiles. Potential risks may include mild muscle soreness associated with exercise and gastrointestinal discomfort related to the supplement.

brief_summary:
Stenosis of the internal carotid artery (ICA) is a common cause of ischemic stroke. Current clinical guidelines focus primarily on the degree of stenosis to determine treatment strategies, such as medical management, endovascular stenting, or surgical endarterectomy. However, the morphology and tissue composition of plaques are increasingly recognized as critical factors for stroke risk, as even mild-to-moderate stenosis may harbor dangerous, vulnerable plaques at risk of rupture. Conventional imaging modalities, such as duplex sonography, provide limited information regarding specific plaque characteristics and vessel wall inflammation, making the discrimination between atherosclerotic and inflammatory diseases a persistent diagnostic challenge. This study utilizes multi-spectral optoacoustic tomography (MSOT), a non-invasive imaging approach that combines ultrasound with laser technology to visualize disease-specific tissue biomarkers. MSOT offers the advantage of assessing specific tissue components, including lipid content, water, collagen, and oxygenation status (oxy- and deoxyhemoglobin), which serve as key indicators of plaque instability, vascularization, and inflammation.

The primary goal of this project is to evaluate the clinical utility of MSOT biomarker signals in characterising carotid plaques and inflammatory vessel wall changes. Investigators aim to find a definitive relation between these tissue-specific MSOT signals within the carotid artery, carotid plaques, and the superficial temporal artery, and relate them to the type (atherosclerosis versus inflammation) and severity of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease. The study encompasses both patients with manifest cardiovascular disease and healthy subjects with cardiovascular risk factors to explore applications in both advanced disease characterization and primary prevention.
primary_outcomes: Multispectral optoacoustic tomography (MSOT) signal intensity of carotid tissue components
National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score
title: Multispectral Optoacoustic Imaging (MSOT) to Investigate Cerebrovascular Disease

brief_summary:
The goal of this study is to see if a daily supplement called Lembas Edge™ helps control appetite and fullness in healthy adults who are overweight. The main questions it aims to answer are:

1. Does taking Lembas Edge™ help reduce hunger and improve feelings of fullness (appetite and satiety)?
2. How does the supplement affect body weight, body mass index (BMI), waist size, food cravings ("food noise"), and digestion?

Researchers will compare two different doses of Lembas Edge™ to a placebo (a pill that looks identical but contains no active supplement) to see how well it works.

Participants will be asked to:

1. Take the study supplement or placebo twice a day (once in the morning and once in the afternoon) for 6 months, with an option to continue in an "open label extension" for an extra 3 months
2. Log their daily meals and snacks and confirm when they take their product using a smartphone app
3. Weigh themselves and check their body composition weekly using a special scale provided by the study
4. Answer weekly and monthly surveys about their hunger levels, food thoughts, digestion, and any health symptoms

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial was to learn whether a six-week mindfulness program, added to standard diabetes treatment, improves blood sugar control, heart rate variability (a measure of how the nervous system regulates the heart), anxiety, and depression in adults aged 18 to 60 years with type 2 diabetes. The main questions it aimed to answer were:

* Does the mindfulness program lower glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting blood glucose, and 2-hour postprandial blood glucose?
* Does it improve heart rate variability, cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction status, and anxiety and depression scores?

Researchers compared participants who received standard therapy plus the mindfulness program with participants who received standard therapy alone.

Participants in the mindfulness group listened to weekly audio-guided practices sent through WhatsApp (mindful eating, breathing exercise, body scan, mindful walking, dealing with unpleasant experiences, and loving-kindness meditation) and were asked to practice daily for six weeks. All participants had blood tests, a 3-minute heart rate variability recording, and the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale questionnaire at the start of the study and after six weeks.
title: Mindfulness Program for Blood Sugar Control, Heart Rate Variability, Anxiety, and Depression in Type 2 Diabetes

brief_summary:
This clinical trial studies how well advanced imaging-guided standard dose versus (vs.) dose-intensified radiation therapy (RT) and dose-intensified accelerated RT works in treating patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma. Radiation therapy uses high energy x-rays, particles, or radioactive seeds to kill tumor cells and shrink tumors. During dose-intensified RT, a higher dose than normal of radiation therapy is delivered over 6 weeks. During dose-intensified accelerated RT, the higher dose of radiation therapy is delivered over a shorter amount of time (2 weeks) than normal (6 weeks). Patients also undergo an advanced brain imaging positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) scan (using a radioactive drug called either FET or FDOPA) prior to RT to that may help doctors better plan the treatment. Dose-intensified and dose-intensified accelerated radiation therapy may be effective in treating patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma. Giving dose-intensified RT or dose-intensified accelerated RT guided by advanced imaging may work better than standard dose RT in treating patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma.

interventions: Dose-intensified Accelerated Photon Beam Radiation Therapy

brief_summary: This is an investigator-initiated, multicenter, observational ambispective cohort study, predominantly retrospective, with an optional prospective non-interventional silent validation. The study tests a cross-scale hypothesis that the pathological micro-niche of the primary prostate tumor (tumor epithelium, invasive front, immune-rich or immune-poor regions, ECM/collagen remodeling, neurovascular neighborhoods, and peritumoral field effect) is associated at the patient level with the imaging macro-niche captured by multiparametric MRI (diffusion, perfusion, heterogeneity, local invasion) and PSMA PET/CT (receptor expression, whole-body lesion distribution, tumor burden). A pathology teacher model provides patient- or lesion-set-level niche representations only during model development; at deployment and validation, only MRI, PSMA PET/CT, and clinical information available before the prediction time point are used, with no voxel-level pathology-to-imaging registration. Under one master protocol with three pre-specified substudies, the system predicts: (A) patient- and lesion-level clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa, ISUP Grade Group 2 or higher) from pre-biopsy MRI; (B) pathological pelvic lymph node metastasis (pN1) after radical prostatectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection, primarily from MRI; and (C) concurrent distant metastasis (M1) and subsequent distant metastasis in baseline M0 patients, primarily from PSMA PET/CT. Models are evaluated for discrimination, calibration, clinical net benefit, uncertainty, abstention, and stability across centers, scanners, tracers, and disease spectra, using locked multicenter external validation and prospective silent validation. Model outputs are never shown to clinicians or patients and do not alter care.
primary_outcomes: Patient-Level Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer (Grade Group 2 or Higher)
Synchronous Distant Metastasis (M1) at Baseline Staging
title: Pathological Micro-Niches and Multimodal Imaging Macro-Niches for Predicting Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer and Metastasis: A Multicenter Study

brief_summary:
Impacted mandibular third molars (wisdom teeth that cannot fully erupt) may damage the adjacent second molar, causing decay on its back surface, loss of the supporting bone or resorption of its root. These problems are often silent and are detected late. This retrospective observational study aims to identify which radiographic features of the impacted third molar are associated with a higher risk of pathology in the second molar.

The study uses panoramic radiographs (OPG) and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) scans that were previously obtained for clinical reasons at the UCAM Dental University Clinic (Murcia, Spain) between 2018 and 2026. No new images or procedures are performed on patients. The position, angulation, depth and contact of the third molar with the second molar are measured, and their relationship with second molar pathology is analysed. The study also compares the information provided by OPG and CBCT and develops and validates a semi-automated, artificial intelligence-based platform to help clinicians make these radiographic measurements faster and more consistently.

This clinical trial uses a study drug (NP-101) alone in some parts of the study or with a recommended treatment for GEP-NEC called Nivo/Ipi (a combination of Nivolumab and Ipilimumab) in other parts of the study and tests it against Placebo (look alike capsules with no active drug) with Nivo/Ipi. The study is divided into three parts. Participants will participate in only one of 3 study parts: Part 1- Dose escalation or Part 2 - Dose selection or Part 3 - Selected dose continuation.

The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if NP-101 (the study drug) can help people with poorly differentiated GEP-NEC live longer; the study includes males and females, age 18 and older who agree to join the study and who qualify.

The main questions the study seeks to answer:

1. Is the study drug in combination with Nivo/Ipi safe?

3. How does the body process the study drug with and without food?
4. Can the study drug plus Nivo/Ipi (the recommended treatment) help people with GEP-NEC live longer than people who do not take the study drug, but who do receive recommended treatment?

Participants will be asked to report how they are feeling, allow for blood draws, body scans, visit the clinic for testing, allow for removal of tumor tissue, take study drug or capsules without medication (along with the recommended treatment) and other procedures which will be explained, along with the study visit schedule, in detail by the study staff before agreeing to participate.

Blood samples will be collected at scheduled time points to measure semaglutide concentrations and compare how the two products are absorbed and eliminated from the body. Safety will also be assessed through adverse events, physical examinations, vital signs, electrocardiograms, and laboratory tests.

brief_summary:
This study aims to evaluate the effects of an earthquake literacy education program on earthquake literacy and earthquake-related fear among middle school students in grades 5-8 in Akpınar district, Kırşehir, Türkiye.

Earthquakes are an important public health concern, and providing children with age-appropriate information may help them understand earthquake risks, develop appropriate preparedness behaviors, and manage earthquake-related fear.

In this study, students will be assigned to either an intervention group or a control group at the class level, with randomization stratified by grade. Students in the intervention group will participate in a three-week earthquake literacy education program. Students in the control group will not receive this education program during the study period.

Earthquake literacy and earthquake-related fear will be assessed using standardized measurement instruments before the intervention (Week 1) and immediately after the intervention (Week 5). Changes in the scores between these two assessments will be compared between the intervention and control groups.

The findings are expected to provide information about the effectiveness of earthquake literacy education in improving students' earthquake literacy and addressing earthquake-related fear.
primary_outcomes: Change in Earthquake Literacy Scale Score
Change in Earthquake Fear Scale Score
title: Effect of Earthquake Literacy Education on Earthquake Literacy and Fear Among Adolescents

brief_summary:
The Artificial Intelligence Assisted Innovative Low-cost Skin Testing Model to Accelerate Person-centered TB Prevention Services in Tanzania, Mozambique and Uganda (TEST4TPT) project will evaluate a person-centered approach to improve access to tuberculosis infection (TBI) testing and linkage to tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) in Mozambique, Tanzania, and Uganda. The project will generate evidence on the feasibility, acceptability, clinical utility, diagnostic and operational performance, and implementation of a novel point-of-care TBI testing approach, including home- or community-based testing and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted reading. By bringing testing closer to people at increased risk of tuberculosis (TB), TEST4TPT aims to reduce barriers to care, support timely TPT initiation, and contribute to improved completion of preventive treatment.

The overall goal of TEST4TPT is to evaluate an integrated, home-based approach to TBI testing using SIILTIBCY (an authorized diagnostic skin test used to detect TBI), community health worker (CHW)-facilitated support, and AI-assisted result reading, with the aim of improving initiation and completion of TPT among close contacts of people newly diagnosed with pulmonary TB disease.
interventions: Standard-of-care TB contact investigation and TPT assessment
Home-based SIILTIBCY testing with SmartPatch/TBConnect AI-assisted reading, conditional on Sub-study 1 results
SmartPatch reading using the TBConnect AI-assisted interpretation
primary_outcomes: Number of eligible contacts initiating tuberculosis preventive treatment per index TB patient
title: Artificial Intelligence Assisted Innovative Low-cost Skin Testing Model to Accelerate Person-centered TB Prevention Services in Tanzania, Mozambique and Uganda

brief_summary: Delayed neurocognitive recovery (dNCR) is a common neurological complication in adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). Emerging evidence suggests that CPB-associated hypoperfusion and perioperative stress remodel the gut microbiome and impair intestinal barrier integrity, which may contribute to neuroinflammation and cognitive decline via the gut-brain axis. This prospective observational cohort study aims to investigate the longitudinal trajectories of the gut metagenome (specifically focusing on Holdemanella biformis and amino acid metabolic functions), fecal and plasma metabolites (L-lysine, L-tryptophan, tryptophanol, and short-chain fatty acids), and plasma markers of intestinal barrier injury (I-FABP) and endotoxin response (LBP) from pre-operation (T0) to post-operation (T2) in adult CPB patients, and to evaluate their associations with postoperative dNCR and domain-specific cognitive changes.
interventions: Longitudinal Biospecimen Collection and Cognitive Assessment
primary_outcomes: Change in Global Cognitive Composite Z-Score (Delta-Z)
title: Gut Microbiota and Amino Acid Metabolism in Post-CPB Delayed Neurocognitive Recovery

brief_summary:
The goal of this observational study is to determine whether fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2) expression in testicular tissue differs between men with non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) who have successful and unsuccessful sperm retrieval during microdissection testicular sperm extraction (micro-TESE).

The main questions it aims to answer are:

1. Does FGF2 expression differ between participants with and without successful sperm retrieval?
2. Is FGF2 expression associated with lower levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) in the blood?
3. Is FGF2 expression associated with higher levels of luteinizing hormone (LH) and total testosterone in the blood, larger testicular volume, and higher Johnsen scores, which reflect sperm development in testicular tissue?
4. Is FGF2 expression associated with OCT4 and VASA, markers found in cells involved in sperm production?
5. Can FGF2 expression help predict whether sperm retrieval will be successful?

Participants will be adult men with NOA who undergo micro-TESE at the participating hospitals. Researchers will:

1. Collect clinical information and review blood hormone test results.
2. Measure testicular volume and examine testicular tissue to assess sperm development.
3. Analyze testicular tissue obtained during micro-TESE to measure FGF2, OCT4, and VASA gene expression using a laboratory method called quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR).
4. Examine testicular tissue under a microscope to determine whether sperm are found.
5. Compare results between participants with and without successful sperm retrieval and assess relationships between FGF2 expression and other clinical, hormonal, and tissue findings.

The findings may improve understanding of sperm production in men with NOA and help researchers investigate whether FGF2 can serve as a marker of sperm retrieval success.
primary_outcomes: Difference in Testicular FGF2 Gene Expression Between Positive and Negative Sperm Retrieval Groups
title: Differences in FGF2 Levels by Sperm Retrieval Success in Non-Obstructive Azoospermia

brief_summary: The proposal combines clinical research in physiotherapy, traumatology and orthopaedics with artificial intelligence, computer vision and health-data science.
title: Artificial Intelligence-assisted Ultrasound Diagnosis of Musculoskeletal Injuries.

brief_summary:
Athletes often increase the amount and intensity of their training for short periods to improve performance. When balanced with adequate recovery, this can lead to beneficial adaptations. However, excessive or poorly managed increases in training can result in non-functional overreaching or overtraining syndrome, where recovery may take weeks, months or even years. These conditions can be associated with reduced athletic performance, poor sleep, low mood and an increased susceptibility to infections. Identifying early indicators of maladaptation to intensive training is therefore important for protecting athletes' health and performance.

Stress hormones, particularly cortisol and testosterone, play important roles in regulating the body's response to exercise and supporting immune function. Previous research suggests that although resting levels of these hormones may remain relatively unchanged following intensified training, their responses to subsequent exercise can become reduced. This may indicate an altered stress response and could have implications for immune function. However, the effects of intensified training on specific immune cells, particularly dendritic cells (DCs), remain poorly understood.

DCs play an important role in recognising infections and activating the body's immune defences. They use specialised receptors, called Toll-like receptors (TLRs), to recognise viral genetic material and trigger the production of immune signalling proteins called cytokines. These responses help coordinate the body's defence against infection. Changes in stress hormones, particularly cortisol, may influence how DCs recognise and respond to potential infections. Consequently, changes in hormone responses following intensified training could affect the ability of these immune cells to function effectively.

The aim of this study is to investigate how a nine-day period of intensified training affects hormonal responses and immune function in recreationally active males and females. The study will measure cortisol and testosterone in saliva and blood, assess changes in circulating immune cell numbers, including T cells and DCs, and investigate the expression and function of DC Toll-like receptors and the production of cytokines following immune stimulation.

It is hypothesised that nine days of intensified training will blunt the normal cortisol and testosterone responses to an acute exercise and alter the changes in circulating T-cell and DC numbers following exercise. It is also hypothesised that intensified training will impair DC responses to immune stimulation, resulting in altered TLR activity and reduced or dysregulated production of cytokines.

Overall, this study aims to improve understanding of how short periods of intensified training affect hormonal regulation and immune function, potentially helping identify early biological indicators of inadequate recovery and increased susceptibility to illness in physically active individuals.
primary_outcomes: T cell and Dendritic cell counts
Dendritic cell toll like receptor 7, 8 and 9 expression
T cell (interleukin-10) and Dendritic cell (Tumor necrosis factor-a and interferon-a) cytokine expression
title: The Effects of a 9-day Intensified Training Period on Immune and Endocrine Biomarkers of Overtraining in Healthy Males and Females.

brief_summary:
Shoulder and upper extremity surgery causes severe postoperative pain. The interscalene brachial plexus block is the standard regional analgesia technique, but it causes ipsilateral hemidiaphragmatic paralysis (HDP) in almost all patients because of its proximity to the phrenic nerve. This can lead to dyspnea, hypoxemia, and atelectasis, especially in obese, elderly, or respiratory-compromised patients. The superior trunk block (STB) has been proposed as a phrenic-sparing alternative, yet HDP still occurs in about 70-76% of patients.

The Shoulder Posterior Pericapsular Nerve Group (SPENG) block is a novel pericapsular technique that targets the articular branches of the suprascapular and axillary nerves with a single injection posterior to the scapula, far from the brachial plexus and phrenic nerve. No randomized controlled trial has yet compared the SPENG block with the STB.

The aim of this prospective, randomized controlled trial is to compare preoperative ultrasound-guided SPENG block and STB in adult patients undergoing elective shoulder and upper extremity surgery under general anesthesia. The primary outcome is the incidence of hemidiaphragmatic paralysis, assessed by M-mode ultrasound measurement of diaphragmatic excursion in the post-anesthesia care unit. Secondary outcomes include intraoperative mechanical power and respiratory mechanics, intraoperative nociception (qNOX) and additional opioid requirement, Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain scores and rescue analgesic consumption during the first 24 postoperative hours, and patient satisfaction.

The investigators hypothesize that the SPENG block will significantly reduce the incidence of hemidiaphragmatic paralysis compared with the STB while providing similar analgesic quality during the first 24 postoperative hours.
lead_sponsor: Bursa Yuksek Ihtisas Training and Research Hospital
title: SPENG Block Versus Superior Trunk Block for Shoulder Surgery: Effects on Diaphragmatic Function, Mechanical Power, Nociception, and Analgesia: A Randomized Controlled Trial

brief_summary:
Study purpose

The goal of this study is to investigate whether adding cervical proprioceptive training to conventional physiotherapy improves cervical sensorimotor control and functional recovery in patients with chronic cervical radiculopathy.

The study will include 58 participants, aged 35-50 years, with unilateral chronic cervical radiculopathy associated with lower cervical discogenic or spondylotic changes (C5-C6 and/or C6-C7), with symptoms lasting more than three months.

Main research questions

1. Does cervical proprioceptive training, in addition to conventional physiotherapy, improve cervical joint position sense (measured by cervical joint position error) compared with conventional physiotherapy alone?
2. Does adding cervical proprioceptive training lead to greater improvements in functional disability, pain intensity, functional ability, and cervical range of motion compared with conventional physiotherapy alone?

Comparison groups

Researchers will randomly allocate participants into two groups:

* Experimental group: Participants will receive conventional physiotherapy combined with a structured cervical proprioceptive training programme.
* Control group: Participants will receive conventional physiotherapy alone.

The researchers will compare the two groups to determine whether adding cervical proprioceptive training produces greater improvements in cervical sensorimotor control and functional outcomes.

What participation involves

Participants will be asked to:

* Complete baseline assessments, including the Neck Disability Index (NDI), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), cervical joint position error (JPE), cervical range of motion (CROM), and Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS).
* Attend their assigned physiotherapy programme three times per week for six weeks, with treatment sessions lasting approximately 60 minutes.
* Follow the treatment programme assigned to their group.
* Complete the same outcome assessments after the six-week intervention period to evaluate changes and compare the results between groups.
title: Effect of Proprioceptive Training on Cervical Sensorimotor Control and Functional Recovery in Patients With Cervical Radiculopathy

The study includes three parts: Part A is single ascending dose in healthy volunteers; Part B is multiple ascending dose in healthy volunteers; Part C is multiple-dose exploration in obese adult participants. Subjects will be randomly assigned to receive IPG1094 or matching placebo. Safety, blood drug concentration and weight-related indicators will be followed up.
